newsitem.title: ITALY: Scalfaro urges Italy parliament to work on reform.
newsitem.headline: Scalfaro urges Italy parliament to work on reform.

text.p: President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro urged parliament on Wednesday to embark on a long overdue review of the way Italy works, his response to the political bickering that has broken out over constitutional reform.

Scalfaro, speaking to journalists on a visit to the northern town of Piacenza, said Italians had "justified expectations" that changes to the country's creaking parliamentary system and method of government would go ahead.
"I believe this process should begin, to answer an issue that has been under discussion for almost 15 years," he said.

Scalfaro made clear he supported the creation of a special commission made up of members from both houses of parliament to propose ways to end Italy's history of short-lived governments and to revamp its legislative processes.
"I don't see any obstacles," he said, noting that all Italy's political parties had campaigned on a platform of constitutional reform at the last general election in April.
The proposal for a bicameral commission stems from parties which support the centre-left government appointed in May and has qualified backing from the opposition centre-right bloc.
Both houses gave the idea strong backing in votes before the summer recess but the commission cannot start work until the proposal has been ratified in a second ballot, expected next month.
The commission would have until next June to draft proposals for constitutional reform. Parliament would then need at least a further year to endorse them before they could be implemented.
Constitutional reform has dominated recent political debate, exposing tensions not only between the blocs but also among the components on each side of the political divide.

Several political commentators believe the commission could undermine Prime Minister Romano Prodi's broad coalition if its partners find themselves at odds or allied with the opposition on constitutional issues.

Media mogul Silvio Berlusconi's opposition Freedom Alliance has also sought to link cooperation on constitutional reform, which will require a two-thirds majority, with concessions from the government on other issues including the 1997 budget.
It met to discuss reform on Wednesday but has made clear it sees little chance of success for a bicameral commission and prefers the election of a special constituent assembly.

Talk of reform has quickened as a result of separatist campaigning by the Northern League party, which declared its own "republic of Padania" in affluent northern Italy last month in a move that exploited deep discontent with inefficient government.

Added impetus has come from a Constitutional Court ruling, made known on Tuesday, that will severely limit the government's powers to use cabinet emergency decrees to legislate in order to get around snail's pace law-making in parliament.
The ruling confronts Prodi with the immediate challenge of convincing parliament to clear a backlog of more than 50 decrees awaiting conversion into law.
In the longer term, it also means that parliament will have to review its structure and provisions for the passage of legislation, which can take years to get on to the statute books.
